study.title: Psalm 147 Praise to the God who restores, sustains, and reveals his word
study.overview: This psalm repeatedly calls the people to praise the LORD because he is worthy of worship and because his goodness is manifested in various spheres: in the restoration of Jerusalem, in the care of the slaughtered, in the government over creation, in the daily provision and in the special revelation given to Israel. The text unites three reasons of praise: God acts in the history of his people, governs nature with power and communicates through his word and his judgments. The tone of the psalm is of reverent gratitude: to praise is not optional, but adequate, pleasurable and just before who God is and what he does.

outline.title: Invitation to praise and restoration of the wounded
outline.explanation: The psalm begins with a direct call to praise the Lord and presents concrete reasons: he rebuilds Jerusalem, brings together the scattered and heals those with broken hearts. Praise is born from the experience of divine restoration and consolation.

outline.title: The greatness of God in creation and daily care
outline.explanation: Here God is described as the one who knows the stars by name, is immeasurably wise, raises up the meek and humbles the wicked. Then the psalmist highlights his providence in the rain, the grass, the food of the animals and the sustenance of who fears in him and awaits his goodness.

outline.title: The protection of Zion and the strength of his word
outline.explanation: Jerusalem and Zion are summoned to praise because God strengthens their doors, blesses their children, guarantees peace to borders and nourishes the people. The psalm then magnifies the vision: God's command runs fast on the earth, showing that his word is effective and sovereign.

outline.title: God's government on winter and revelation to Israel
outline.explanation: Snow, frost and ice appear as acts of the Creator, and the cold only undoes when he sends his word and wind. The psalm ends by stating that God made known to Jacob his statutes and judgments in a singular way, which distinguishes Israel from other nations and concludes with a new call to praise.

study.context: The provided notes likely situate the psalm in the post-cative period when Jerusalem was being restored and fortified. It is also possible, according to a commentator, to relate certain expressions to the construction and strengthening of Jerusalem in the previous time. The text, however, does not depend on a closed date to fulfill its purpose: it celebrates God's action in the restoration of his people and in the community life of Zion.
study.theology: Theologically, the psalm presents God as creator, sustainer, governor of history and revealer of his will. He is not only powerful in cosmic terms; his power leans toward the poor, the meek and those who wait in him. The text also states that human strength and natural resources are not the ultimate foundation of the security of God's people; the right trust lies in the goodness of the LORD. Moreover, the revelation of his judgments to Israel is a unique privilege: God not only acts, but also speaks. Thus, the psalm unites providence and revelation, nature and covenant, worship and obedience.

scholarViews.insight: The call of 147:1 is an invitation to worship, linking praise to the concrete reasons presented in the psalm.
Praise is due because God restored Jerusalem and gathered the scattered, a reason for community gratitude.
In 147:2, the psalmist seems to see the walls being erected while the exiles are gathered for the work.

questions: What concrete motives does the psalm present so that praise is more than a momentary emotion?
How does this psalm correct confidence in human force, material resources or own capacity?
How should the idea that God has revealed his judgments to Israel to shape our obedience today?
study.practice: Pray with this psalm recognizing three things: the restoration you received from God, the care of him in the daily needs and the authority of your word over your life. Then choose an area in which you have trusted more in human media than in the Lord and give this area to it in prayer and practical obedience. It is also appropriate to turn praise into community action: thank God with other believers for signs of restoration and provision.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not allow to safely affirm the authorship, the exact date or the definitive historical scenario of the psalm. The reference to the post-cative period is likely, not certain. It is also not possible to conclude with certainty whether the mentions of Jerusalem and Zion should be read only as a literal restoration of the city or also in a broader and more symbolic way; the text allows both readings, without the notes requiring a final solution.
